title: Asser’s problem
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal: For every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over a finite relational vocabulary, does there exist a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over some finite relational vocabulary such that, for every positive integer \(n, \psi\) has a model with exactly n elements if and only if \(\varphi\) has no model with exactly n elements?
definitions: A vocabulary is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified positive integer arity; the list and the arities may vary with the sentence and are not bounded by a fixed global constant. Equality is allowed. Sentences use variables, relation atoms, equality, Boolean connectives and first-order quantification, with no free variables. A finite model has a nonempty domain A and interprets each k-ary relation as a subset of \(A^{k}\), with equality interpreted as equality on A. The spectrum \(Spec(\varphi )\) is {\(n\in N:n\ge 1\) and some finite model of \(\varphi\) has cardinality n}. The required equality is \(Spec(\psi )=N_{>0}\) minus \(Spec(\varphi )\). The vocabulary of \(\psi\) need not be the vocabulary of \(\varphi\). No bound on the length of \(\psi\) and no effective transformation \(\varphi \mapsto \psi\) are required. Restricting to relational vocabularies loses no ordinary first-order spectra: functions and constants can be represented by their graph relations with first-order axioms for totality and uniqueness. This is closure of the class of spectra, not a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Determine a basic closure property of finite first-order expressibility after taking possible model sizes.

importance.reason: A classical foundational question of finite model theory and descriptive complexity, explicitly surveyed as an unresolved central spectrum problem. Its complement target is distinct from PTIME capture, query containment and ordinary finite satisfiability.

progress.text: Asser formulates whether complements of spectra are spectra, as documented in the historical survey.
The comprehensive survey retains the general complement question among its unresolved problems.

context_blocks.text: A spectrum forgets the internal structure of a model and remembers only its possible finite sizes. A sentence can impose substantial combinatorial conditions on its relations, but the resulting object is just a subset of the positive integers. Asser’s question asks whether sizes excluded by one finite description can themselves be the allowed sizes of another finite description.

Negating the sentence does not solve the problem. If \(\varphi\) describes a graph consisting of disjoint edges covering all vertices, its spectrum contains the positive even numbers. An even-sized edgeless graph nevertheless satisfies \(\neg \varphi\), so even numbers also belong to \(Spec(\neg \varphi )\). Existence of a countermodel at a given size is different from absence of every model at that size.

The quantifier order is therefore essential. The target permits a new sentence \(\psi\), chosen after \(\varphi\) but before n, which represents the entire complement simultaneously. It is not enough to provide a separate sentence for each excluded size. Allowing \(\psi  a\) different vocabulary also prevents an arbitrary choice of representation from imposing an unintended extra restriction.

The spectrum problem helped shape finite model theory and descriptive complexity. The survey by Durand, Jones, Makowsky and More records Asser’s complement question as unresolved and connects the subject with bounded computational resources and structural restrictions on models. The importance here is the closure operation on the full expressive class, rather than one particular encoding of a graph family.

The existing logic-for-PTIME card asks for a logical characterization of efficient properties of individual finite structures. This card instead concerns the sets of cardinalities admitting some structure satisfying a sentence. It adds a different foundational question to the database and finite-model-theory bucket, even though both connect logic with computation.
